newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Marcos decree brings cheer to Chinese fishermen.
newsitem.headline: Marcos decree brings cheer to Chinese fishermen.

text.p: Twenty-one Chinese fishermen held for 52 days in the Philippines cheered on Thursday after hearing they were finally sailing home -- thanks to a martial law decree by the late Ferdinand Marcos.

"You will soon be free... The Chinese embassy will not abandon you," embassy second secretary Wang Haitao told them after a Philippine judge dismissed illegal entry charges against them and ordered their release.
The fishermen, some in rumpled clothes, applauded.

Wang was one of two Chinese diplomats who boarded the Chinese fishing boat with a delegation of Filipino-Chinese businessmen to inform the fishermen of Judge Eliodoro Ubiadas's decision and to bring them food.
The fishermen were arrested by the Philippine Navy on May 20 in the South China Sea near a rock formation, called Scarborough Shoal, that both Manila and Beijing claim.
Their arrest was one of a series of incidents that have
soured relations between Manila and Beijing, which have staked rival claims over islands in the South China Sea.
A decree issued by then-president Marcos in 1978 under his martial law powers was used to free the fishermen.

Ubiadas said the decree defined the Philippines' exclusive economic zone as 200 nautical miles, but where it overlaps another country's zone, the issue must be resolved by an agreement among the countries concerned or in accord with international law.

The judge said it had not been shown that ownership of the shoal had been resolved, so "there can be no legal basis as yet for the conclusion that the accused...entered Philippine territory illegally".
Marcos was ousted after 20 years in power by a popular revolt in 1986, but a number of his martial law edicts remain in force. He died in exile in Hawaii in 1989.
Major Enrique Romero, police chief of Subic town where the Chinese are detained aboard their boat, said he expected to free the fishermen later on Thursday after formalities were completed.
Beijing says all isles, reefs and shoals in the South China Sea historically belong to China. Manila says the shoal is within its exclusive economic zone and that it has sole sovereignty over it.
The shoal lies well north of the Spratly islands, a cluster of potentially oil-rich isles, shoals and atolls that Beijing says have also been Chinese territory since ancient times.
The Spratlys are also claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, Taiwan, the Philippines, Malaysia and Brunei.
